newsitem.title: UK: British lottery creates 193 new millionaires.
newsitem.headline: British lottery creates 193 new millionaires.

text.p: Britain's national lottery raised 1.44 billion pounds ($2.4 billion) for good causes last year and created 193 new millionaires, its regulator Peter Davis said on Thursday.

Davis said the success of the lottery had been greater than expected and, based on current projections over the seven-year licence term, the total contribution to good causes was likely to reach 30 percent of sales.

"The future is bright for the National Lottery," he said in his annual report for 1996/97. "As the impact from proceeds from the good cases continues to be felt across the country, it is clear that we can all count ourselves as winners."

The most controversial winners of the lottery -- the executives from lottery operator Camelot Group Plc have sparked a bitter row with the new Labour government over bonus payments that had inflated Camelot's wage bill by 40 percent to 2.3 million pounds.
At the same time, the sum the lottery raised for good causes fell.
But the row was diffused after the executives agreed earlier this month to hand over some of their future bonuses to charity in a concession.

Davis, who wants to increase his regulatory powers, also said he had asked Chris Smith, the minister responsible for the lottery, to extend his powers to fine Camelot if it breaches its licence terms.
He declined to detail the size of any fine he was seeking, adding that this was a matter for the minister.

"The level of the penalty that is necessary is one that will reflect the gravity of a licence breach but will also be meaningful to a substantial business with turnover of five billion pounds per annum," he told BBC radio.

Davis cannot currently impose fines. He has powers of reference to the courts or, as a last resort, can revoke a licence. But these are actions which can only be taken in what he calls "the most serious situations".
Davis said the lottery had given away 2.26 billion pounds over the year in prizes -- accounting for 48 percent of lottery revenues.
Good cases accounted for 30 percent of revenues, lottery duty for 12 percent and retailers as well as Camelot operating costs and profit accounted for only five percent, he said.
Around 95 percent of adults in Britain are believed to have bet on the lottery and nearly 70 percent of adults play the on-line game regularly, spending on average 2.50 pounds each we week.
Launched in 1994, the lottery is played regularly by millions in Briton who dream of winning jackpots which can top 10 million pounds.
But critics have described it a "tax on the poor" and attacked Camelot for its big profits and "fat cat" executive salaries.

The government plans to publish next month details of plans to plough one billion pounds of lottery funds into health and education projects over the next five years. The money is expected to come from a midweek draw launched earlier this year.
The government will also outline its plans to give the lottery to a non-profit operator when Camelot's licence expires in 2001.
The lottery operator, owned by Cadbury Schweppes Plc, De La Rue Plc, GTECH UK, Racal Electronics Plc and ICL, is to discuss with the government how a non-profit operator might work.
Smith has said Camelot would be considered a candidate to run the reformed lottery when its licence expires.
($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
